candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 31 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 32 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 33 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 34 not required. 35
candidates.context: This guidance describes frequently encountered issues to consider in early drug development and 26 pre-IND meetings including topics related to pharmaceutical quality, nonclinical evaluation, 27 clinical pharmacology, and clinical development including early phase study designs and 28 statistical analysis plans. 29 1 This guidance has been prepared by the Office of New Drugs in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research in cooperation with Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research at the Food and Drug Administration.

candidates.statement: Issues discussed during pre-IND meetings may vary depending on the drug, program 56 development stage, and targeted disease. For standard 59 pre-IND meeting package elements, see the draft guidance for industry Formal Meetings 60 Between the FDA and Sponsors or Applicants of PDUFA Products . 5

candidates.statement: The FDA can exercise flexibility in determining which clinical pharmacology studies are 191 essential to inform the safe and effective use of a drug, whether integrated with clinical efficacy 192 and safety trials or conducted separately in healthy subjects, as well as which clinical 193 pharmacology studies may be deferred until after a drug is approved. Sponsors should be 194 familiar with the expectations for including clinical pharmacology information in a new drug 195 application. See the References section for a list of relevant guidance documents that may be 196 helpful in planning the clinical pharmacology aspects of the drug development program. 197
candidates.context: Although studies in healthy subjects may determine which factors influence a drug’s disposition 183 or pharmacodynamic effects, dedicated clinical trials that inform dosing and usage instructions in 184 the target population with a rare disease may be limited. Therefore, careful planning of the 185 clinical pharmacology aspects of the drug development plan for a rare disease is important, 186 because information from such studies and analyses can inform trial design and serve as 187 supportive evidence of effectiveness. candidates.statement: Sponsors developing drugs for rare diseases face many challenges. These may include the small 230 number of disease-affected individuals, lack of understanding of the natural history of the 231 disorder, lack of precedent for drug development (e.g., established clinical endpoints, validated 232 biomarkers), phenotypic heterogeneity, and the need to conduct trials in pediatric populations, 233

Although FDA has no specified minimum number of patients needed to establish drug safety and 239 efficacy, the number of patients should be adequate to assess benefit and risk. While the 240 approval standard for drugs treating rare diseases is the same as that for drugs treating nonrare 241 diseases, it is appropriate for FDA to exercise the broadest possible scientific judgment in 242 applying the evidentiary standard in the rare disease setting. candidates.statement: Although FDA has no specified minimum number of patients needed to establish drug safety and 239 efficacy, the number of patients should be adequate to assess benefit and risk. While the 240 approval standard for drugs treating rare diseases is the same as that for drugs treating nonrare 241 diseases, it is appropriate for FDA to exercise the broadest possible scientific judgment in 242 applying the evidentiary standard in the rare disease setting. To that end, FDA will consider: (1) 243 benefits and risks of the drug; (2) seriousness of the disease; and (3) if there is an unmet medical 244 need. This approach reflects FDA’s recognition that patients and physicians are generally 245 willing to accept greater risks and side effects from treatment of life-threatening and severely 246 debilitating diseases than they would for other diseases. 13

candidates.statement: The Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA), as amended and codified in section 505B of the 353 FD&C Act, requires sponsors of certain new drug applications (NDAs) or biologics license 354 applications (BLAs) and certain supplements to such applications to submit an assessment of the 355 safety and effectiveness of the drug in pediatric patients at the time the application is submitted, 356 unless the requirement has been deferred or waived. 20 An initial pediatric study plan (iPSP) is 357 required to be submitted within 60 days of an end of phase 2 meeting, 21 and an agreed-upon iPSP 358 must be included with submission of an NDA or BLA. However, for serious and life-threatening 359 diseases (including rare diseases), FDA encourages sponsors to submit their plans for pediatric 360 product development as early as feasible before initiating pediatric studies. Some drugs may be 361 exempted from requirements under PREA, such as certain drugs that have orphan drug 362 designation. 22 Nevertheless, FDA encourages sponsors to submit pediatric study plans for all 363 drugs intended for pediatric indications (including drugs exempted from the requirement) to help 364 facilitate pediatric drug development. 365
